extracted.intended_audience: toxicologists, risk assessors, regulatory agency staff, and AEGL authors/reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and review criteria for developing Acute Exposure Guideline Levels (AEGLs) for airborne chemicals, and the NRC committee's criteria for evaluating NAC-prepared AEGL reports. Covers evidence types, dose‑response selection, uncertainty factors, endpoints, carcinogenic risk estimation, and procedural review steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL concept and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGLs represent threshold exposure limits for the general public applicable to emergency exposures ranging from 10 minutes to 8 hours. They apply to the general population, including susceptible subpopulations (infants, children, elderly, persons with asthma or other illnesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGL values are threshold levels below which adverse health effects are not likely to occur for the general public. They are intended for planning, response, and prevention across community, workplace, transportation, military, and remediation contexts. Note that idiosyncratic individual responses may occur at concentrations below the AEGL.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL exposure periods and levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Three AEGL levels (AEGL-1, AEGL-2, AEGL-3) are developed for five exposure periods: 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, 4 h, and 8 h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each AEGL level corresponds to increasing severity of effects across the specified exposure durations; values should be established for all five time points when data permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL-1 definition
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL-1 is the airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience notable discomfort, irritation, or certain asymptomatic nonsensory effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects at or above AEGL-1 are not disabling and are transient and reversible upon cessation of exposure. AEGL-1 represents mild, progressive, transient, nondisabling sensory irritation or certain asymptomatic nonsensory adverse effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL-2 definition
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL-2 is the airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience irreversible or other serious, long-lasting adverse health effects or an impaired ability to escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGL-2 denotes concentrations associated with significant health impairment or functional impairment that could hinder escape.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL-3 definition
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL-3 is the airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience life-threatening adverse health effects or death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGL-3 identifies concentrations associated with life‑threatening effects or mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and review all relevant published and unpublished information including: (1) chemical‑physical characterizations, (2) structure‑activity relationships, (3) in vitro toxicity studies, (4) animal toxicity studies, (5) controlled human studies, (6) observations of humans involved in chemical accidents, and (7) epidemiologic studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toxicity data from human studies are most applicable and preferred when available. Use a weight‑of‑evidence approach integrating these data types to set AEGL values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for human and inhalation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Toxicity data from human studies are used in preference to animal and in vitro data; toxicity data from inhalation exposures are most useful for setting AEGLs because inhalation is the most likely route of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using non-inhalation data, recognize additional uncertainty in extrapolation to inhalation exposures and document rationale for extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal-to-human extrapolation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When human data are unavailable, toxicity data from laboratory animals are extrapolated to estimate potential human toxicity; use species most representative of humans in pharmacodynamic/pharmacokinetic properties, or, if unavailable, the most sensitive species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrapolation requires experienced scientific judgment. Consider pharmacokinetic data on tissue doses when available to inform interspecies extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and magnitude of uncertainty factors (UFs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty factors are commonly used when animal data are used to estimate human risk levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magnitude of UFs depends on the quality of the animal data used to determine the NOAEL (no‑observed‑adverse‑effect level) and the substance's mode of action. Document justification for chosen UFs and their magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of multiple endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: For substances that affect several organ systems or have multiple effects, all endpoints (including reproductive [both genders], developmental, neurotoxic, respiratory, and other organ‑related effects) must be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most important or most sensitive effect should receive greatest attention when deriving AEGLs; justify selection of critical effect/end point for each AEGL level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to carcinogenic chemicals
rubrics_metrics.description: For carcinogens, estimate excess carcinogenic risk and derive AEGLs corresponding to specified risk levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate AEGLs corresponding to excess risks of 1 in 10,000 (1 × 10−4), 1 in 100,000 (1 × 10−5), and 1 in 1,000,000 (1 × 10−6) exposed persons and document methods and assumptions used.

rubrics_metrics.name: First step: comprehensive data collection and review
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in establishing AEGLs for a chemical is to collect and review all relevant published and unpublished information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically search for and evaluate available data across evidence types, and document data gaps and rationale for data selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL report development team composition and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL draft reports are prepared by ad hoc AEGL development teams consisting of a chemical manager, two chemical reviewers, and a staff scientist of the NAC contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly attribute roles and responsibilities in the report and ensure the development team documents methods, data, and reasoning used to derive AEGLs.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL report review and public comment process
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft AEGL documents are reviewed by NAC, elevated to 'proposed' status, published in the Federal Register for public comment, revised by NAC in response to public comments, and moved to 'interim' status before NRC final evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the staged process (draft → proposed → interim → final), document responses to public comments, and ensure transparency of revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: NRC committee review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The NRC Committee on Acute Exposure Guideline Levels evaluates AEGL reports for scientific validity, completeness, and consistency with NRC guideline reports (e.g., NRC 1993, 2001a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee provides advice and recommendations for revisions, requests oral and written presentations from report authors, and iteratively reviews revised reports until satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and reliance on source data accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the large volume of data, the NRC committee cannot verify all data used by NAC and relies on NAC for the accuracy and completeness of toxicity data cited in AEGL reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document data sources and quality; recognize this limitation in review and, where possible, identify critical data elements that reviewers should verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to emergency exposure contexts distinct from occupational/ambient limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing occupational or ambient exposure limits are not easily or directly translated into emergency exposure limits for high‑level, short‑duration exposures (often less than 1 hour) for the general population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGLs are specifically designed for once‑in‑a‑lifetime emergency exposures across vulnerable populations and should be derived using AEGL procedures rather than by adapting workplace/ambient standards.
